NE-1.t: Describe neurulation, including notochord induction of the neural plate, elevation and fusion of the neural folds, and closure of the anterior and posterior neuropores during the fourth week.
NE-1.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: neural tube defects

NE-1.t: Relate the primary brain vesicles (prosencephalon, mesencephalon, rhombencephalon) and secondary vesicles (telencephalon, diencephalon, mesencephalon, metencephalon, myelencephalon) to the adult structures and ventricles each forms.

Distinguish neuroectoderm derivatives (CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma, retina) from neural crest derivatives (sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes) and mesoderm-derived microglia.

Distinguish spina bifida occulta, meningocele, myelomeningocele, and anencephaly, and relate open neural tube defects to elevated maternal serum and amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein and to periconceptional folate deficiency.
NE-1.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: neural tube defects

NE-1.t: Explain holoprosencephaly as failed separation of the prosencephalon into two hemispheres, linked to sonic hedgehog pathway defects and trisomy 13, and relate it to midline facial defects such as cyclopia and cleft lip.
NE-1.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: neural tube defects (holoprosencephaly)

NE-1.t: Compare Chiari I malformation (cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum, associated with syringomyelia), Chiari II malformation (vermis and medulla herniation with lumbosacral myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus), and Dandy-Walker malformation (vermis agenesis with cystic fourth ventricle).
NE-1.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: hydrocephalus, obstructive (Arnold-Chiari)

NE-2.t: Identify the parts of a multipolar motor neuron (soma with Nissl substance, dendrites, axon hillock, axon, synaptic terminals) and compare it with pseudounipolar dorsal root ganglion neurons and bipolar retinal and olfactory neurons.

Describe the connective tissue layers of a peripheral nerve (endoneurium around each axon, perineurium around each fascicle, epineurium around the whole nerve) and explain the perineurium's role as a blood-nerve barrier.

Compare myelination by Schwann cells (one internode of one axon in the PNS) and oligodendrocytes (internodes of many axons in the CNS), and relate Schwann cell injury to Guillain-Barré syndrome and oligodendrocyte injury to multiple sclerosis and PML.
NE-2.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: multiple sclerosis

NE-2.t: Identify the functions of astrocytes (blood-brain barrier support, potassium buffering, glial scar), microglia (resident CNS macrophages that form multinucleated giant cells in HIV infection), and ependymal cells lining the ventricles.

Describe Wallerian degeneration distal to an axon transection and central chromatolysis in the cell body, and explain why peripheral axons can regenerate along Schwann cell tubes while CNS axons generally do not.
NE-2.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial and peripheral nerve disorders: peripheral nerve injury

NE-2.t: Identify red neurons (shrunken cell body, eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus) as the histologic marker of irreversible neuronal injury, appearing about 12 to 24 hours after hypoxia or ischemia.
NE-2.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: anoxic brain damage, cerebral hypoxia

NE-3.t: Locate the primary motor, primary somatosensory, primary visual, and primary auditory cortices and the Broca and Wernicke areas, and predict the deficit produced by a lesion of each.

Describe the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, including dopamine acting on D1 and D2 receptors, and predict how loss of substantia nigra pars compacta neurons (Parkinson disease) or caudate neurons (Huntington disease) changes movement.
NE-3.usmle: Nervous System: Movement disorders: Parkinson disease, Huntington disease

NE-3.t: Explain cerebellar function in coordination and distinguish a vermis lesion (truncal ataxia, wide-based gait) from a hemisphere lesion (ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia).

Identify the thalamic relay nuclei (VPL for body sensation, VPM for face sensation and taste, LGN for vision, MGN for hearing, VL for motor) and relate thalamic infarction to contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.
NE-3.usmle: Nervous System: Neurologic pain syndromes: thalamic pain syndrome

NE-3.t: Identify the brainstem level of the cranial nerve nuclei (midbrain III and IV; pons V to VIII; medulla IX, X, XII) and the spinal cord's gray horns, white columns, enlargements, and conus medullaris ending near L1 to L2.

Explain how damage to the ascending reticular activating system of the upper brainstem or to both cerebral hemispheres causes coma, and distinguish coma, delirium, and brain death (irreversible loss of all brain and brainstem function).
NE-3.usmle: Nervous System: Global cerebral dysfunction: altered states of consciousness, delirium, coma, brain death

NE-4.t: Describe the meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia) and the epidural, subdural, and subarachnoid spaces, and identify which space an arterial epidural, venous subdural, and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage occupies.
NE-4.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: epidural and subdural hematoma

NE-4.t: Identify the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and predict the structures compressed in subfalcine (anterior cerebral artery), uncal (CN III, posterior cerebral artery, cerebral peduncle), and tonsillar (medullary respiratory centers) herniation.
NE-4.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: disorders of increased intracranial pressure

NE-4.t: Describe the subarachnoid cisterns, including the lumbar cistern below the conus medullaris where lumbar puncture is done at L3 to L4 or L4 to L5, and the arachnoid granulations that return CSF to the dural venous sinuses.

Explain the blood-brain barrier (endothelial tight junctions, basement membrane, astrocyte foot processes) and the blood-CSF barrier (choroid plexus epithelium), and identify circumventricular organs that lack a barrier, such as the area postrema and posterior pituitary.

Interpret CSF opening pressure, cell count and type, protein, and glucose to distinguish bacterial, viral, fungal, and tuberculous meningitis, and recognize albuminocytologic dissociation in Guillain-Barré syndrome.

NE-5.t: Classify Meissner corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles, Merkel discs, Ruffini endings, free nerve endings, muscle spindles, and Golgi tendon organs by stimulus, adaptation rate, and afferent fiber type.
Trace the dorsal column medial lemniscus and spinothalamic pathways from receptor to cortex, naming where each decussates, and predict the sensory loss from a lesion at a given level.
NE-5.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal cord compression

NE-5.t: Predict the findings of Brown-Séquard hemisection (ipsilateral weakness and loss of vibration and position sense, contralateral loss of pain and temperature) and syringomyelia (bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch).
NE-5.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: syringomyelia

NE-5.t: Describe the monosynaptic stretch reflex (spindle, Ia afferent, alpha motor neuron), the Golgi tendon organ Ib reflex, and the withdrawal and crossed extensor reflexes, and identify the roots of the biceps (C5), triceps (C7), patellar (L4), and Achilles (S1) reflexes.

Explain referred pain as convergence of visceral and somatic afferents on the same spinal segments, using cardiac pain felt in the left arm and diaphragmatic irritation felt in the shoulder (C3 to C5) as examples.

Explain pain modulation by gate control and by descending inhibition from the periaqueductal gray using endogenous opioids, and identify postherpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain, and thalamic pain as neuropathic pain from nervous system injury.
NE-5.usmle: Nervous System: Neurologic pain syndromes: postherpetic neuralgia, phantom limb pain

NE-5.t: Distinguish migraine (unilateral pulsating headache with nausea and photophobia, often with aura, involving trigeminovascular activation and CGRP release), cluster headache (brief severe periorbital pain with ipsilateral lacrimation and rhinorrhea), and tension headache (bilateral band-like pressure).
NE-5.usmle: Nervous System: Paroxysmal disorders: headache, including migraine, cluster, tension

NE-6.t: Trace the visual pathway from retina through optic nerve, chiasm, optic tract, lateral geniculate nucleus, and optic radiations (Meyer loop) to the calcarine cortex, and predict the visual field defect from a lesion at each site.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: injury to optic nerve and pathways

NE-6.t: Describe the pupillary light reflex (CN II afferent, Edinger-Westphal nucleus and CN III efferent) and accommodation, and interpret anisocoria, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and an Argyll Robertson pupil.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: anisocoria, miosis, mydriasis

NE-6.t: Explain phototransduction in rods and cones (light isomerizing retinal in rhodopsin, transducin activation, cGMP breakdown by phosphodiesterase, closure of cGMP-gated sodium channels, hyperpolarization) and relate vitamin A deficiency to night blindness.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: night blindness

NE-6.t: Describe aqueous humor production by the ciliary epithelium and drainage through the trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm, and describe tear film production by the lacrimal gland (CN VII parasympathetic fibers) and meibomian glands.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: glaucoma, lacrimal system disorders

NE-6.t: Trace sound transmission through the tympanic membrane, ossicles, oval window, and cochlea, explain hair cell transduction in potassium-rich endolymph and tonotopy (base high frequency, apex low), and distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss with Weber and Rinne tests.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: hearing loss

NE-6.t: Describe the semicircular canals (angular acceleration), utricle and saccule (linear acceleration and gravity), and vestibulo-ocular reflex, and relate vestibular imbalance to vertigo and nystagmus and sensory conflict to motion sickness.
NE-6.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: disorders of balance, motion sickness, nystagmus

NE-6.t: Trace taste (CN VII anterior two thirds, CN IX posterior third, to the nucleus solitarius and VPM) and smell (olfactory neurons through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, no thalamic relay), and predict anosmia after cribriform fracture.

NE-7.t: Trace the lateral corticospinal tract from the precentral gyrus through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, and pyramidal decussation to the anterior horn alpha motor neuron.

Distinguish upper from lower motor neuron lesions by tone, reflexes, Babinski sign, fasciculations, and atrophy, and apply this to ALS (mixed signs) and poliomyelitis and spinal muscular atrophy (lower motor neuron signs).
NE-7.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, spinal muscular atrophy

NE-7.t: Compare the one-neuron somatic motor pathway (acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors of skeletal muscle) with the two-neuron visceral motor pathway (preganglionic and postganglionic neurons) to smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

Predict the findings of subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts), tabes dorsalis (dorsal columns and dorsal roots), anterior spinal artery infarction (dorsal columns spared), and complete cord transection.
NE-7.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal artery infarct, spinal cord transection

NE-7.t: Describe visceral sensory pathways, including pain afferents that travel with sympathetic nerves and reflex afferents from carotid sinus baroreceptors (CN IX) and aortic arch baroreceptors (CN X) to the nucleus solitarius.

NE-8.t: Identify each cranial nerve's skull foramen, components, and functions, and predict the deficit from injury, such as a down-and-out eye with ptosis and mydriasis (CN III), failed abduction (CN VI), or tongue deviation toward the lesion (CN XII).
NE-8.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: cranial nerve injury

NE-8.t: Distinguish a central (upper motor neuron) facial lesion that weakens only the contralateral lower face from a CN VII lesion that weakens the entire ipsilateral face, including the forehead.
NE-8.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: Bell palsy

NE-8.t: Describe the brachial plexus (roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches) and predict deficits from Erb palsy (C5 to C6), Klumpke palsy (C8 to T1), and injuries to the axillary, radial, median, ulnar, and long thoracic nerves.
NE-8.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: peripheral nerve injury, including brachial plexus

NE-8.t: Predict deficits from injuries to lower limb nerves: common fibular at the fibular neck (foot drop), tibial, femoral, obturator, and superior gluteal (Trendelenburg sign).
NE-8.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: peroneal tunnel syndrome

NE-8.t: Use dermatome landmarks (C6 thumb, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 knee and medial leg, L5 dorsum of foot, S1 lateral foot) to localize a spinal nerve root lesion.

Explain internuclear ophthalmoplegia from a medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion (impaired adduction on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye, convergence preserved) and its association with multiple sclerosis.
NE-8.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: internuclear ophthalmoplegia

NE-9.t: Compare sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1 to L2) and parasympathetic (craniosacral, CN III, VII, IX, X and S2 to S4) outflow, including where preganglionic and postganglionic cell bodies and ganglia lie.

Identify the transmitter and receptor at each autonomic synapse (acetylcholine at nicotinic ganglia, norepinephrine at adrenergic targets, acetylcholine at muscarinic targets and sweat glands) and the G protein linked to alpha1, alpha2, beta, M1, M2, and M3 receptors.

Trace the oculosympathetic pathway (hypothalamus, ciliospinal center at C8 to T2, superior cervical ganglion, carotid plexus) and predict ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis in Horner syndrome from a Pancoast tumor or carotid dissection.
NE-9.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: Horner syndrome, ptosis of the eyelid

NE-9.t: Identify the parasympathetic ganglia of the head and their targets: ciliary (CN III, pupillary sphincter and ciliary muscle), pterygopalatine (CN VII, lacrimal gland), submandibular (CN VII, submandibular and sublingual glands), and otic (CN IX, parotid).

Explain autonomic dysreflexia after spinal cord injury at or above T6, linking a stimulus below the lesion (such as a full bladder) to unopposed sympathetic discharge with severe hypertension and reflex bradycardia.
NE-9.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: autonomic dysreflexia

NE-10.t: Trace the circle of Willis from the internal carotid and vertebrobasilar systems and identify the territories supplied by the anterior, middle, and posterior cerebral arteries and the lenticulostriate arteries.
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: cerebral artery occlusion

NE-10.t: Predict the stroke syndrome from occlusion of the ACA (contralateral leg), MCA (contralateral face and arm, aphasia if dominant, neglect if nondominant), PCA (homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing), and lenticulostriate arteries (pure motor lacunar stroke).
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: stroke, thrombotic and embolic

NE-10.t: Predict brainstem syndromes from occlusion of the PICA (lateral medullary syndrome with dysphagia, hoarseness, and crossed pain loss), anterior spinal artery (medial medullary syndrome), AICA (lateral pontine syndrome), and basilar artery (locked-in syndrome).
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: vertebral artery deficiency

NE-10.t: Trace CSF from the choroid plexus through the interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, and foramina of Luschka and Magendie to the subarachnoid space, and predict which ventricles dilate with obstruction at each site.
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: hydrocephalus

NE-10.t: Describe venous drainage through the dural venous sinuses to the internal jugular veins, and relate tearing of bridging veins to subdural hematoma and dural sinus thrombosis to raised intracranial pressure.
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: venous sinus thrombosis

NE-10.t: Explain autoregulation of cerebral blood flow and its sensitivity to PaCO2 (hypercapnia dilates, hypocapnia constricts), and use cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP minus ICP) to explain the Cushing reflex of hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing.
NE-10.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: disorders of increased intracranial pressure

NE-11.t: Describe prefrontal association cortex functions (executive function, planning, judgment, personality) and predict disinhibition, apathy, and poor judgment after frontal lobe damage, as in frontotemporal dementia.
NE-11.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: frontotemporal dementia

NE-11.t: Explain the role of parietal association cortex in spatial attention, and predict hemispatial neglect after a nondominant (usually right) parietal lesion and Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right confusion) after a dominant angular gyrus lesion.

Distinguish Broca aphasia (nonfluent, comprehension intact), Wernicke aphasia (fluent, comprehension impaired), conduction aphasia (repetition impaired, arcuate fasciculus), and global aphasia by lesion site.

Compare the dorsal (occipitoparietal, spatial location and motion) and ventral (occipitotemporal, object and face recognition) visual association streams, and predict prosopagnosia after fusiform gyrus damage.
Relate EEG patterns to arousal and sleep stages (beta awake, alpha relaxed with eyes closed, theta in N1, sleep spindles and K complexes in N2, delta in N3, low-voltage beta-like activity in REM).

NE-12.t: Identify hypothalamic nuclei and functions: supraoptic and paraventricular (ADH, oxytocin), arcuate (dopamine, GHRH), lateral (hunger), ventromedial (satiety), anterior (heat loss), posterior (heat conservation), and suprachiasmatic (circadian rhythm).

Explain hypothalamic thermoregulation, including how pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) raise the set point through prostaglandin E2 in fever, and predict hyperphagia after ventromedial lesions and anorexia after lateral lesions.

Describe the limbic system (hippocampus, amygdala, cingulate gyrus, fornix, mammillary bodies) and relate hippocampal damage to anterograde amnesia, mammillary body damage to Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, and bilateral amygdala damage to Klüver-Bucy syndrome.
NE-12.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B1 (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome)

NE-12.t: Explain how the suprachiasmatic nucleus, driven by retinal light input, sets circadian rhythm through pineal melatonin, and relate loss of lateral hypothalamic orexin (hypocretin) neurons to narcolepsy with cataplexy.
NE-12.usmle: Nervous System: Sleep disorders: cataplexy and narcolepsy, circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder

NE-12.t: Distinguish REM sleep behavior disorder (loss of REM atonia, often preceding Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia), N3 parasomnias of childhood (sleepwalking, sleep terrors), and restless legs syndrome (urge to move at rest, linked to iron deficiency).
NE-12.usmle: Nervous System: Sleep disorders: REM sleep behavior disorder, sleep terror disorder, restless legs syndrome

NE-13.t: Explain the resting membrane potential using the Na+/K+ ATPase, potassium leak channels, and the Nernst equation, and predict how changes in extracellular potassium alter neuronal and muscle excitability.

Describe the phases of the action potential (voltage-gated sodium channel activation and inactivation, delayed potassium efflux, afterhyperpolarization), threshold, and the absolute and relative refractory periods.
Compare graded potentials (EPSPs and IPSPs) with action potentials and explain temporal and spatial summation at the axon hillock.

Explain how myelin speeds conduction by saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier, how axon diameter affects velocity, and why demyelination in multiple sclerosis and Guillain-Barré syndrome slows or blocks conduction.
NE-13.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: multiple sclerosis

NE-13.t: Describe neuromuscular transmission (calcium entry, SNARE-mediated vesicle release, acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors, acetylcholinesterase) and predict how botulinum toxin, myasthenia gravis, and Lambert-Eaton syndrome each disrupt it.
NE-13.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: myasthenia gravis

NE-13.t: Classify seizures as focal (with or without impaired awareness) or generalized (tonic-clonic, absence with 3 Hz spike-and-wave), explain them as excess synchronous neuronal firing from an excitation and inhibition imbalance, and describe febrile seizures in young children.
NE-13.usmle: Nervous System: Paroxysmal disorders: seizure disorders, absence, partial, febrile seizures

NE-13.t: Explain hypokalemic periodic paralysis as an inherited skeletal muscle ion channelopathy causing episodes of flaccid weakness with low serum potassium, often triggered by carbohydrate-rich meals or rest after exercise.
NE-13.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: muscle channelopathies (hypokalemic periodic paralysis)

NE-14.t: Explain why the brain depends on glucose (entering through GLUT1 at the blood-brain barrier and GLUT3 on neurons) and shifts to ketone bodies in prolonged fasting, and predict neuroglycopenic symptoms of hypoglycemia.

Explain thiamine pyrophosphate as a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase, and relate deficiency to Wernicke encephalopathy, dry beriberi, and worsening when glucose is given before thiamine.
NE-14.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B1, thiamine

NE-14.t: Explain vitamin B12 as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, and use elevated methylmalonic acid to distinguish B12 deficiency, which damages myelin, from folate deficiency, which spares the nervous system.
NE-14.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B12, cobalamins

NE-14.t: Relate neurologic findings to deficiencies of vitamin B6 (seizures and neuropathy from impaired GABA and transmitter synthesis), niacin (pellagra with dementia), and vitamin E (spinocerebellar ataxia and dorsal column degeneration).
NE-14.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B3, B6, E

NE-14.t: Explain how hyperammonemia from liver failure or urea cycle defects injures the brain, linking astrocyte glutamine synthetase activity to astrocyte swelling and Alzheimer type II astrocytes.
NE-14.usmle: Multisystem: Inborn errors of metabolism: urea cycle diseases

NE-14.t: Describe the lipid composition of myelin (cholesterol, galactocerebroside, sulfatide, sphingomyelin) and relate defects in lysosomal sphingolipid breakdown to neurodegeneration in the sphingolipidoses and leukodystrophies.
Explain how lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, and relate lead poisoning to encephalopathy in children and to wrist and foot drop from peripheral motor neuropathy in adults.

NE-15.t: Trace catecholamine synthesis from tyrosine through L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate limiting), dopamine, norepinephrine (dopamine beta-hydroxylase, vitamin C dependent), and epinephrine (PNMT, induced by cortisol).

Describe catecholamine breakdown by MAO and COMT to homovanillic acid (from dopamine) and vanillylmandelic acid and metanephrines (from norepinephrine and epinephrine), and relate elevated urinary HVA and VMA to neuroblastoma.
Trace serotonin synthesis from tryptophan by tryptophan hydroxylase in the raphe nuclei, its conversion to melatonin in the pineal gland, and its breakdown by MAO to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.

Explain GABA synthesis from glutamate by pyridoxal phosphate-dependent glutamate decarboxylase, contrast glutamate (excitatory, NMDA and AMPA receptors) with GABA and glycine (inhibitory), and relate glutamate excitotoxicity to ischemic neuronal death.

Describe acetylcholine synthesis by choline acetyltransferase from acetyl-CoA and choline and its breakdown by acetylcholinesterase, and relate loss of cholinergic neurons in the nucleus basalis of Meynert to Alzheimer disease.
NE-15.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: Alzheimer disease

NE-15.t: Identify the main source nuclei of dopamine (substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area), norepinephrine (locus coeruleus), and serotonin (raphe), and relate decreased dopamine to Parkinson disease and decreased GABA and acetylcholine to Huntington disease.
NE-15.usmle: Nervous System: Movement disorders: Parkinson disease, Huntington disease

NE-16.t: Explain trinucleotide repeat expansion in Huntington disease (CAG, HTT), fragile X syndrome (CGG, FMR1 hypermethylation), myotonic dystrophy (CTG, DMPK), and Friedreich ataxia (GAA, frataxin), including each inheritance pattern and anticipation in the first three.
NE-16.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic disorders: triplet repeat disorders, fragile X syndrome

NE-16.t: Explain the chromosomal mechanisms of Down syndrome (maternal meiotic nondisjunction, Robertsonian translocation, mosaicism) and relate an extra copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21 to early-onset Alzheimer disease.

Explain how loss of tumor suppressor genes causes autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndromes: NF1 (neurofibromin, chromosome 17), NF2 (merlin, chromosome 22), tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 hamartin, TSC2 tuberin, mTOR activation), and von Hippel-Lindau (VHL, chromosome 3).
NE-16.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease

NE-16.t: Describe Sturge-Weber syndrome as a sporadic somatic GNAQ mutation causing a facial port-wine stain in the CN V1 distribution, ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and glaucoma.
NE-16.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: Sturge-Weber syndrome

NE-16.t: Explain spinal muscular atrophy as autosomal recessive loss of SMN1 causing degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons, with a floppy infant, tongue fasciculations, and areflexia in the severe infantile form.
NE-16.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: spinal muscular atrophy

NE-16.t: Relate driver gene defects to nervous system tumors: two-hit RB1 tumor suppressor loss in retinoblastoma, IDH mutation with 1p/19q codeletion in oligodendroglioma, and MYCN oncogene amplification predicting aggressive neuroblastoma.
NE-16.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: neoplasms: retinoblastoma

NE-17.t: Describe the hypophyseal portal system and the hypothalamic hormones (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) that control the anterior pituitary, and explain why dopamine is the main inhibitor of prolactin.

Explain ADH and oxytocin synthesis in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei with axonal transport to the posterior pituitary, and predict central diabetes insipidus or SIADH after head trauma, neurosurgery, or a CNS tumor.
Predict the effects of a pituitary adenoma or craniopharyngioma compressing the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and pituitary stalk (hyperprolactinemia from loss of dopamine inhibition).
Explain the neuroendocrine stress response linking the hypothalamus to the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla (catecholamines) and to the HPA axis (CRH, ACTH, cortisol).

Relate thyroid hormone to nervous system function, including impaired brain development in congenital hypothyroidism, delayed reflex relaxation in hypothyroidism, and tremor and hyperreflexia in hyperthyroidism.

NE-18.t: Describe how the blood-brain barrier and resident microglia shape CNS innate immunity, and explain how cytokine release (IL-1, TNF) in bacterial meningitis increases barrier permeability and causes cerebral edema.
NE-18.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, bacterial

NE-18.t: Explain multiple sclerosis as T cell-mediated (Th1 and Th17) autoimmune injury to CNS myelin, with HLA-DR2 association, CSF oligoclonal IgG bands, and periventricular white matter plaques.
NE-18.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: multiple sclerosis

NE-18.t: Explain molecular mimicry in Guillain-Barré syndrome after Campylobacter jejuni infection, with antibodies against peripheral nerve gangliosides, and relate anti-GQ1b antibodies to the Miller Fisher variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia).
NE-18.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: Guillain-Barré syndrome, Miller Fisher syndrome

NE-18.t: Classify myasthenia gravis (antibodies to postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, associated with thymoma and thymic hyperplasia) and Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels) as type II hypersensitivity, and MS and ADEM as T cell-mediated.
NE-18.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: myasthenia gravis, including thymoma

NE-18.t: Explain neurologic paraneoplastic syndromes as immune responses to tumor antigens shared with neurons: anti-Hu (small cell lung cancer, sensory neuronopathy, limbic encephalitis), anti-Yo (cerebellar degeneration), and anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (ovarian teratoma).

Explain how conjugate polysaccharide vaccines against H. influenzae type b, S. pneumoniae, and N. meningitidis produce T cell-dependent responses, and compare inactivated (Salk) with live oral (Sabin) polio vaccines for mucosal IgA immunity.

NE-19.t: Compare the morphology and capsule-based virulence of Streptococcus pneumoniae (gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci), Neisseria meningitidis (gram-negative diplococci with lipooligosaccharide endotoxin), and Haemophilus influenzae type b (gram-negative coccobacillus with polyribosylribitol phosphate capsule).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, bacterial

NE-19.t: Describe the neonatal meningitis pathogens Streptococcus agalactiae (group B, maternal vaginal colonization), Escherichia coli with the K1 capsule, and Listeria monocytogenes (gram-positive rod, tumbling motility, actin-based cell spread, unpasteurized dairy and deli meats).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, bacterial

NE-19.t: Contrast botulinum toxin (cleaves SNARE proteins, blocking acetylcholine release and causing flaccid paralysis) with tetanospasmin (retrograde transport to spinal inhibitory interneurons, blocking GABA and glycine release and causing spastic paralysis).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: botulism, tetanus

NE-19.t: Describe DNA viruses of the nervous system: herpesviruses (enveloped dsDNA, latency in sensory ganglia, spread along axons) and JC polyomavirus (nonenveloped dsDNA, latent in the kidney, reactivated in immunosuppression).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: encephalitis, CNS disorders associated with AIDS

NE-19.t: Describe RNA viruses of the nervous system: enteroviruses (nonenveloped positive-sense picornaviruses, fecal-oral), West Nile virus (flavivirus spread by Culex mosquitoes from bird reservoirs), and rabies virus (bullet-shaped negative-sense rhabdovirus, retrograde axonal transport).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, viral; encephalitis

NE-19.t: Identify Cryptococcus neoformans (encapsulated yeast in pigeon droppings, seen with India ink, detected by capsular antigen), Mucor and Rhizopus (broad nonseptate hyphae favored by ketoacidosis), and Coccidioides (spherules, southwestern US soil).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, fungal

NE-19.t: Compare Treponema pallidum (spirochete detected with darkfield, VDRL, and FTA-ABS), Borrelia burgdorferi (spirochete spread by Ixodes ticks), and Mycobacterium leprae (acid-fast, prefers cooler body sites, infects Schwann cells, armadillo reservoir in the US).
NE-19.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, spirochetal

NE-20-A.t: Distinguish thrombotic cerebral infarction (atherosclerosis at the carotid bifurcation, MCA, or basilar artery) from embolic infarction (cardiac sources such as atrial fibrillation, often with hemorrhagic conversion) and lacunar infarcts from hypertensive arteriolosclerosis.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: stroke, thrombotic and embolic

NE-20-A.t: Describe the time course of cerebral infarction: red neurons by 12 to 24 hours, neutrophils in the first days, macrophages clearing debris over weeks, and reactive gliosis around a fluid-filled cyst from liquefactive necrosis.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: cerebral infarction

NE-20-A.t: Distinguish ischemic stroke, hemorrhagic stroke, and transient ischemic attack by mechanism, list shared risk factors (hypertension, atrial fibrillation, diabetes, smoking, dyslipidemia), and explain why noncontrast CT is used first to exclude hemorrhage.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: transient ischemic attack, stroke

NE-20-A.t: Explain global hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy, identifying the most vulnerable neurons (hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, neocortical pyramidal cells with laminar necrosis) and watershed infarcts between arterial territories after severe hypotension.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: anoxic brain damage, cerebral hypoxia

NE-20-A.t: Compare epidural hematoma (middle meningeal artery tear with temporal bone fracture, lucid interval, biconvex and limited by sutures) with subdural hematoma (bridging vein tear in elderly, alcohol use, or shaken infants, crescent-shaped and crossing sutures).
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma

NE-20-A.t: Explain subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured saccular aneurysm, most often near the anterior communicating artery, with sudden worst headache and xanthochromic CSF, risk factors ADPKD and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and complications vasospasm and hydrocephalus.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: subarachnoid hemorrhage, cerebral artery aneurysm

NE-20-A.t: Explain hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms in the basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, and cerebellum, and contrast it with lobar hemorrhage from cerebral amyloid angiopathy in older adults.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: intracerebral hemorrhage

NE-20-A.t: Describe the spinal cord blood supply (one anterior and two posterior spinal arteries, artery of Adamkiewicz) and predict anterior spinal artery syndrome after aortic surgery or dissection: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature with vibration and position sense spared.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal artery thrombosis, embolus, infarct

NE-20-A.t: Describe arteriovenous malformations (tangles of arteries draining directly into veins without a capillary bed) and other vascular malformations as causes of intracerebral hemorrhage and seizures in young adults.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: arteriovenous malformations, ectatic cerebral vessels

NE-20-A.t: Explain carotid and vertebral artery dissection as a cause of stroke in young adults after neck trauma, and subclavian steal syndrome (proximal subclavian stenosis reversing vertebral flow, with arm claudication and unequal arm blood pressures).
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: carotid and vertebral dissection, subclavian steal syndrome

NE-20-A.t: Explain cerebral venous sinus thrombosis in hypercoagulable states such as pregnancy and estrogen use, and hypertensive encephalopathy and posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome as vasogenic edema, mainly of posterior white matter, during severe hypertension.
NE-20-A.usmle: Nervous System: Cerebrovascular disease: venous sinus thrombosis, hypertensive encephalopathy, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome

NE-20-B.t: Explain Alzheimer disease pathogenesis: amyloid precursor protein cleavage by beta and gamma secretase into amyloid beta plaques, hyperphosphorylated tau tangles, and risk from age, APOE e4, Down syndrome, and APP, PSEN1, or PSEN2 mutations.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: Alzheimer disease

NE-20-B.t: Identify Alzheimer disease findings: cortical atrophy with hydrocephalus ex vacuo, hippocampal involvement, neuritic plaques, neurofibrillary tangles, amyloid angiopathy, and a course beginning with short-term memory loss.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: Alzheimer disease

NE-20-B.t: Explain ALS as degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons (some familial cases with SOD1 or C9orf72 mutations) causing mixed UMN and LMN signs with sensation, bladder control, and eye movements spared, and death from respiratory failure.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Neuromuscular disorders: amyotrophic lateral sclerosis

NE-20-B.t: Explain Parkinson disease as loss of substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons with alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies, causing resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and postural instability, and identify secondary parkinsonism from MPTP and dopamine-blocking drugs.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Movement disorders: Parkinson disease, including Parkinson dementia

NE-20-B.t: Explain Huntington disease as an autosomal dominant CAG expansion in HTT on chromosome 4 with caudate atrophy and GABAergic neuron loss, causing chorea, dementia, and depression in midlife, with anticipation through paternal transmission.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Movement disorders: Huntington disease

NE-20-B.t: Explain Friedreich ataxia (autosomal recessive GAA expansion in frataxin, mitochondrial iron accumulation) as spinocerebellar degeneration of dorsal columns, spinocerebellar and corticospinal tracts, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, diabetes, kyphoscoliosis, and pes cavus.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: Friedreich ataxia

NE-20-B.t: Explain Guillain-Barré syndrome as acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy after infection, causing ascending symmetric flaccid weakness with areflexia, and complications of respiratory failure and autonomic instability.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: Guillain-Barré syndrome

NE-20-B.t: Describe multiple sclerosis risk factors (women aged 20 to 40, higher latitude), relapsing-remitting course, and findings including optic neuritis, internuclear ophthalmoplegia, sensory loss, heat-worsened symptoms, and periventricular MRI plaques.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: multiple sclerosis; optic neuritis

NE-20-B.t: Distinguish acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (monophasic, mostly in children, after viral infection or rarely vaccination, perivenular demyelination) from relapsing multiple sclerosis.

Distinguish dementia with Lewy bodies (cortical Lewy bodies, visual hallucinations, fluctuating cognition, parkinsonism), frontotemporal dementia (early personality change, tau Pick bodies or TDP-43 inclusions), and progressive supranuclear palsy (tau, vertical gaze palsy, early falls).
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: Lewy body disease, frontotemporal dementia, progressive supranuclear palsy

NE-20-B.t: Distinguish vascular dementia (stepwise decline after multiple infarcts or diffuse small vessel disease) and mild cognitive impairment (measurable decline with daily function preserved) from Alzheimer disease.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Degenerative disorders/amnestic syndromes: mild cognitive impairment; Cerebrovascular disease: vascular dementia

NE-20-B.t: Describe transverse myelitis as acute inflammation across a spinal cord segment, often after infection or with MS, causing bilateral weakness, a sensory level, and bladder dysfunction.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: transverse myelitis

NE-20-B.t: Distinguish essential tremor (often familial, postural and action tremor that may improve with alcohol) from parkinsonian resting tremor and cerebellar intention tremor, and describe cervical dystonia (torticollis) as sustained involuntary neck muscle contraction.
NE-20-B.usmle: Nervous System: Movement disorders: essential tremor; torticollis/cervical dystonia

NE-20-C.t: Compare vasogenic edema (blood-brain barrier disruption from tumor, abscess, or trauma), cytotoxic edema (cell swelling from ischemia or hypoxia), and interstitial edema (hydrocephalus), and predict papilledema, Cushing triad, and herniation as complications.
NE-20-C.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: cerebral edema

NE-20-C.t: Distinguish noncommunicating hydrocephalus (aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker, tumor) from communicating hydrocephalus (arachnoid granulation scarring after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage) and from hydrocephalus ex vacuo, and explain head enlargement in infants.
NE-20-C.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: hydrocephalus

NE-20-C.t: Describe normal pressure hydrocephalus in older adults as enlarged ventricles without consistently raised opening pressure, causing urinary incontinence, magnetic gait, and dementia that may improve after CSF drainage.
NE-20-C.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: hydrocephalus, including normal-pressure

NE-20-C.t: Describe idiopathic intracranial hypertension in obese women of childbearing age (headache, papilledema, vision loss, CN VI palsy, normal imaging, raised opening pressure) and its associations with vitamin A excess and tetracyclines.
NE-20-C.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: idiopathic intracranial hypertension

NE-20-D.t: Explain hepatic encephalopathy from ammonia and other gut-derived toxins bypassing the liver in cirrhosis or portosystemic shunts, its precipitants (GI bleeding, infection, high protein intake, constipation, hypokalemia), and findings of confusion and asterixis.
NE-20-D.usmle: Nervous System: Metabolic disorders: metabolic encephalopathy

NE-20-D.t: Classify peripheral neuropathy by pattern (distal symmetric, mononeuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex) and by axonal or demyelinating injury, and list major causes: diabetes, alcohol, B12 and thiamine deficiency, vasculitis, leprosy, HIV, and neurotoxic chemotherapy.
NE-20-D.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: neuropathy, mononeuritis

NE-20-D.t: Explain diabetic neuropathy (sorbitol accumulation, advanced glycation end products, microvascular injury) and its findings: stocking-glove sensory loss, autonomic dysfunction (gastroparesis, orthostatic hypotension), neuropathic foot ulcers, and pupil-sparing CN III palsy.
NE-20-D.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: neuropathy

NE-20-D.t: Identify causes of B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia, strict vegan diet, gastrectomy, ileal disease, Diphyllobothrium latum) and its neurologic findings: subacute combined degeneration with lost vibration and position sense, positive Romberg sign, spasticity, neuropathy, and dementia.
NE-20-D.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B12 (pernicious anemia)

NE-20-D.t: Explain Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ophthalmoplegia, ataxia) and its progression to Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia with confabulation), with mammillary body and medial thalamic damage, in alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, or hyperemesis.
NE-20-D.usmle: Multisystem: Vitamin deficiencies: vitamin B1 (Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome)

NE-20-D.t: Describe Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease as a group of inherited motor and sensory neuropathies (most often autosomal dominant PMP22 duplication) causing distal weakness, foot drop, pes cavus, and hammer toes.
NE-20-D.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease

NE-20-D.t: Explain osmotic demyelination syndrome after overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, with demyelination of the central pons causing quadriparesis, dysarthria, dysphagia, and possible locked-in syndrome.
NE-20-D.usmle: Nervous System: Metabolic disorders: metabolic encephalopathy

NE-20-E.t: Describe the neurologic and associated features of Down syndrome: intellectual disability, hypotonia, early-onset Alzheimer disease, atlantoaxial instability, and associated duodenal atresia, atrioventricular septal defects, and increased leukemia risk.

Compare the leukodystrophies: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1, very long chain fatty acid buildup from impaired peroxisomal oxidation, adrenal insufficiency), metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A, sulfatides), and Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase, globoid cells).

Explain phenylketonuria as autosomal recessive phenylalanine hydroxylase or BH4 deficiency, making tyrosine essential, and relate phenylalanine buildup to intellectual disability, seizures, musty odor, fair skin, and microcephaly in infants of untreated mothers.

Distinguish Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A, GM2 ganglioside, cherry-red macula, no hepatosplenomegaly) from Niemann-Pick disease (sphingomyelinase, cherry-red macula with hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells).

Describe the neurologic features of Fabry disease (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency, painful neuropathy, angiokeratomas, early stroke), Gaucher disease (glucocerebrosidase, neuronopathic types 2 and 3), and Hurler (alpha-L-iduronidase, corneal clouding) versus Hunter syndrome (X-linked, no corneal clouding).
NE-20-E.usmle: Multisystem: Storage diseases: Fabry disease, mucopolysaccharidoses

NE-20-E.t: Explain Wilson disease as autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation impairing biliary copper excretion, with low ceruloplasmin, copper deposits in the basal ganglia causing tremor, dystonia, and psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings, and liver disease.

Describe fragile X syndrome (FMR1 CGG expansion with hypermethylation and silencing) as the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, with autism features, long face, large ears, and macroorchidism.
NE-20-E.usmle: Multisystem: Genetic disorders: fragile X syndrome

NE-20-E.t: Explain maple syrup urine disease (branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase deficiency, sweet urine odor, neonatal encephalopathy) and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency (X-linked hyperammonemia with orotic aciduria) as inborn errors that injure the brain.
NE-20-E.usmle: Multisystem: Inborn errors of metabolism: maple syrup urine disease, urea cycle diseases

NE-20-E.t: Explain acute intermittent porphyria (autosomal dominant porphobilinogen deaminase deficiency) with attacks of abdominal pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric symptoms, elevated urine porphobilinogen, and triggers such as alcohol, fasting, and cytochrome P450 inducers.
Identify causes of congenital microcephaly, including congenital Zika, cytomegalovirus, rubella, and toxoplasma infection, fetal alcohol syndrome, and maternal phenylketonuria.

NE-20-F.t: Describe medulloblastoma as the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood: a small round blue cell tumor of the cerebellum with Homer Wright rosettes that can block the fourth ventricle and seed the CSF as drop metastases.

Describe meningioma as a dural-based extra-axial tumor of arachnoid cap cells, common in adult women, with whorls and psammoma bodies, associations with NF2 and prior radiation, and seizures or focal deficits from compression.

Describe neuroblastoma as a neural crest tumor of young children, usually in the adrenal medulla, presenting as an abdominal mass with elevated urinary HVA and VMA, Homer Wright rosettes, opsoclonus-myoclonus, and worse prognosis with MYCN amplification.

Describe glioblastoma as the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults: an IDH-wildtype astrocytic tumor that can cross the corpus callosum, with pseudopalisading necrosis, microvascular proliferation, GFAP staining, and poor survival.

Distinguish pilocytic astrocytoma (children, cerebellum, cystic with mural nodule, Rosenthal fibers, BRAF alteration, good prognosis) from IDH-mutant diffuse astrocytoma and oligodendroglioma (frontal lobe, fried-egg cells, chicken-wire capillaries, calcification, seizures).

Describe neuronal and mixed neuronal-glial tumors such as ganglioglioma, a slow-growing temporal lobe tumor of children and young adults that presents with seizures, and central neurocytoma within the lateral ventricles.

Describe schwannoma (S-100 positive Schwann cells, Antoni A areas with Verocay bodies and Antoni B areas) and predict hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance from a vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle, bilateral in NF2.
NE-20-F.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: acoustic neuroma, neurofibromatosis type 2

NE-20-F.t: Describe neurofibromatosis type 1: café-au-lait macules, cutaneous neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas with risk of malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, Lisch nodules, optic pathway glioma, and pheochromocytoma.

Describe brain metastases as the most common intracranial tumors in adults (from lung, breast, melanoma, and other primaries, often at the gray-white junction) and primary CNS lymphoma (diffuse large B cell, EBV-related in AIDS).
NE-20-F.usmle: Nervous System: Neoplasms: metastatic; primary CNS lymphoma

NE-20-F.t: Describe retinoblastoma (leukocoria in young children, bilateral in hereditary RB1 cases, later osteosarcoma risk) and uveal melanoma as the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults.
NE-20-F.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: neoplasms: melanoma, retinoblastoma

NE-20-F.t: Describe the CNS lesions of tuberous sclerosis (cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytoma, seizures, with ash-leaf spots and cardiac rhabdomyoma) and von Hippel-Lindau disease (cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma).
NE-20-F.usmle: Nervous System: Congenital disorders: tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease

NE-20-G.t: Describe arboviral encephalitis (West Nile, St. Louis, and eastern and western equine encephalitis viruses) transmitted by mosquitoes from bird reservoirs, with humans as dead-end hosts, and West Nile acute flaccid paralysis in older adults.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: encephalitis, arboviruses

NE-20-G.t: Distinguish foodborne botulism (preformed toxin), infant botulism (ingested spores, honey, floppy baby with constipation), and wound botulism, all causing descending symmetric flaccid paralysis starting with cranial nerves, without fever or sensory loss.

Explain brain abscess spread from contiguous infection (sinusitis, otitis, mastoiditis, dental) or hematogenous seeding (endocarditis, lung infection, right-to-left cardiac shunts), common organisms (streptococci, staphylococci, anaerobes), and a ring-enhancing lesion with fever and focal deficits.

Describe the histology of viral encephalitis (perivascular lymphocytic cuffs, microglial nodules, neuronophagia), and rabies acquired from bat, raccoon, or dog bites, with Negri bodies, agitation, and hydrophobia.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: encephalitis, rabies virus

NE-20-G.t: Describe parasitic CNS infection: Toxoplasma gondii (ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS), Taenia solium neurocysticercosis (ingested eggs, brain cysts, seizures), and Naegleria fowleri (freshwater exposure, cribriform plate entry, rapidly fatal meningoencephalitis).
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: encephalitis, Taenia, Toxoplasma gondii; protozoal meningitis

NE-20-G.t: Describe cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS (raised opening pressure, positive capsular antigen) and rhinocerebral mucormycosis in diabetic ketoacidosis (necrotic nasal or palatal eschar spreading to the orbit and brain).
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, fungal

NE-20-G.t: Distinguish CNS herpesvirus diseases: HSV-1 hemorrhagic temporal lobe encephalitis, HSV-2 meningitis and neonatal encephalitis, CMV encephalitis in advanced AIDS and congenital periventricular calcifications, and EBV-associated primary CNS lymphoma.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: encephalitis, herpesviruses

NE-20-G.t: Compare tuberculoid leprosy (strong Th1 response, few bacilli, few anesthetic hypopigmented plaques, thickened nerves) with lepromatous leprosy (Th2 response, many bacilli, leonine facies, symmetric glove-and-stocking neuropathy).

Identify the common causes of bacterial meningitis by age: group B streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria in neonates; S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis in children and adults; and S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and Listeria in older adults.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, bacterial

NE-20-G.t: Describe the findings and complications of meningitis (fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, petechial rash in meningococcemia, sensorineural hearing loss, hydrocephalus, seizures), including tuberculous basilar meningitis with cranial nerve palsies.

Describe neurosyphilis forms in tertiary syphilis: meningovascular disease, general paresis, and tabes dorsalis (dorsal column and root degeneration with sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign, Argyll Robertson pupils, and Charcot joints), with CSF VDRL testing.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, spirochetal (neurosyphilis)

NE-20-G.t: Explain poliomyelitis as fecal-oral enterovirus infection that spreads to and destroys anterior horn motor neurons, causing asymmetric flaccid paralysis, fasciculations, and areflexia without sensory loss, and later post-polio syndrome.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, viral: polioviruses

NE-20-G.t: Explain prion disease as conversion of normal alpha-helical PrP into protease-resistant beta-pleated PrP (sporadic, inherited, or acquired, including variant CJD from bovine prions), causing rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus, and spongiform change without inflammation.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: prion disease: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

NE-20-G.t: Explain PML as JC virus reactivation in severe immunosuppression (AIDS, natalizumab, rituximab), causing lytic oligodendrocyte infection with multifocal white matter demyelination and rapidly progressive deficits.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: CNS disorders associated with AIDS: progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

NE-20-G.t: Describe subacute sclerosing panencephalitis as a persistent defective measles virus infection appearing years after early childhood measles, causing progressive cognitive decline and myoclonus with high CSF anti-measles antibody levels.

Describe tetanus after spores enter a contaminated wound or the umbilical stump in neonates, causing trismus, risus sardonicus, opisthotonus, and spastic paralysis, and explain prevention by toxoid immunization.

Explain VZV latency in dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia and reactivation as dermatomal herpes zoster, including herpes zoster ophthalmicus, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles), and postherpetic neuralgia.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: herpes zoster

NE-20-G.t: Describe Lyme neuroborreliosis (facial nerve palsy, often bilateral, lymphocytic meningitis, radiculopathy) and leptospirosis acquired from water contaminated by animal urine as spirochetal causes of meningitis.
NE-20-G.usmle: Nervous System: Infectious disorders: meningitis, spirochetal: Borrelia burgdorferi, Leptospira

NE-20-H.t: Describe concussion as trauma-induced transient neurologic dysfunction without structural imaging changes, postconcussion syndrome, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy (dementia pugilistica) with tau deposits after repeated head injury.
NE-20-H.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: traumatic brain injury (concussion), postconcussion syndrome, dementia pugilistica

NE-20-H.t: Explain coup and contrecoup contusions at the frontal and temporal poles and diffuse axonal injury from acceleration-deceleration shearing, which causes axonal swellings and coma without a mass lesion.
NE-20-H.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: traumatic brain syndrome, traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage

NE-20-H.t: Predict the progression of an expanding traumatic hematoma: rising intracranial pressure, uncal herniation with an ipsilateral dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis, secondary Duret hemorrhages in the brainstem, and death without decompression.
NE-20-H.usmle: Nervous System: Traumatic and mechanical disorders: epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, intraparenchymal hemorrhage

NE-20-H.t: Explain the phases of spinal cord transection, from spinal shock (flaccid paralysis, areflexia, neurogenic hypotension) to spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia, and predict ventilator-dependent quadriplegia at or above C3 (phrenic roots C3 to C5) versus paraplegia from thoracic injury.
NE-20-H.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal cord transection, paraplegia, quadriplegia

NE-20-H.t: Distinguish spinal cord compression (back pain, sensory level, upper motor neuron signs) from cauda equina syndrome (saddle anesthesia, urinary retention, lost anal reflex, lower motor neuron signs), caused by metastasis, epidural abscess, or central disc herniation.
NE-20-H.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal cord compression, cauda equina syndrome

NE-20-I.t: Explain Bell palsy as idiopathic lower motor neuron CN VII palsy linked to HSV reactivation, diabetes, pregnancy, and Lyme disease, with whole-face ipsilateral weakness, hyperacusis, loss of anterior tongue taste, and reduced tearing.
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: Bell palsy

NE-20-I.t: Explain carpal tunnel syndrome as median nerve compression under the flexor retinaculum (risks: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, dialysis amyloid), with nocturnal thumb-to-ring finger paresthesia, thenar atrophy, Tinel and Phalen signs, and spared palm sensation.
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: carpal tunnel syndrome

NE-20-I.t: Explain disc herniation as nucleus pulposus protruding through a torn annulus fibrosus, usually posterolaterally at L4 to L5 or L5 to S1, and predict that it compresses the lower root (for example, an L4 to L5 disc affects L5).
Explain radiculopathy from nerve root entrapment by disc, osteophytes, or foraminal narrowing, and predict the dermatomal pain, weakness, and reflex loss of C6, C7, L4, L5, and S1 root lesions.
Describe sciatica as radiating pain from the buttock down the posterior thigh below the knee, usually from L5 or S1 root compression by disc herniation, reproduced by a straight leg raise test.

Explain thoracic outlet syndrome as compression of the lower brachial plexus trunk (C8 to T1), subclavian artery, or vein by a cervical rib or scalene muscles, with ulnar-side hand paresthesia, intrinsic hand weakness, and vascular symptoms.

Explain trigeminal neuralgia as paroxysmal unilateral lancinating facial pain in the V2 or V3 distribution triggered by touch or chewing, usually from vascular compression of the nerve root, and as a sign of MS in younger patients.
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Neurologic pain syndromes: trigeminal neuralgia

NE-20-I.t: Predict the findings of cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve at the elbow, fourth and fifth finger paresthesia, intrinsic weakness), tarsal tunnel syndrome (tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus, sole paresthesia), and common fibular compression at the fibular neck (foot drop).
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Peripheral nerve/plexus injury/disorders: cubital, tarsal, and peroneal tunnel syndromes

NE-20-I.t: Describe lumbar spinal stenosis causing neurogenic claudication (leg pain worse with standing and extension, relieved by sitting or flexion) and cervical stenosis causing myelopathy with upper motor neuron signs.
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders relating to the spine, spinal cord, and spinal nerve roots: spinal stenosis

NE-20-I.t: Describe complex regional pain syndrome (burning pain, allodynia, swelling, and skin and temperature changes after limb injury, with type II following a nerve injury) and phantom limb pain after amputation.
NE-20-I.usmle: Nervous System: Neurologic pain syndromes: complex regional pain syndrome, phantom limb pain

NE-20-J.t: Describe blepharitis (anterior from staphylococcal or seborrheic disease, posterior from meibomian gland dysfunction), and distinguish a painful hordeolum (acute gland infection, usually S. aureus) from a painless chalazion (meibomian lipogranuloma).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: blepharitis, hordeolum, chalazion

NE-20-J.t: Explain cataract as lens protein opacification, with risks of age, diabetes (sorbitol), galactosemia (galactitol), corticosteroids, UV light, smoking, and congenital rubella, causing painless progressive blurred vision, glare, and loss of the red reflex.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: cataract

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish viral conjunctivitis (adenovirus, watery discharge, preauricular node), bacterial conjunctivitis (purulent; hyperacute with N. gonorrhoeae), chlamydial conjunctivitis and trachoma, and allergic conjunctivitis (type I hypersensitivity, itching).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: conjunctivitis (adenovirus), keratoconjunctivitis

NE-20-J.t: Explain glaucoma as optic neuropathy with disc cupping, and contrast open-angle glaucoma (impaired trabecular outflow, painless peripheral vision loss) with acute angle-closure glaucoma (painful red eye, fixed mid-dilated pupil, halos, nausea).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: glaucoma

NE-20-J.t: Describe keratitis (HSV dendritic ulcer; Pseudomonas and Acanthamoeba in contact lens wearers; corneal ulcer risk) and iritis or anterior uveitis (ciliary flush, photophobia, small irregular pupil).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: iridocyclitis, corneal ulcer, keratoconjunctivitis

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish dry macular degeneration (drusen, gradual central vision loss) from wet macular degeneration (VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization, rapid central loss, distortion), with age and smoking as risk factors.

NE-20-J.t: Relate anterior uveitis to HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and posterior uveitis and chorioretinitis to toxoplasmosis and CMV retinitis in AIDS.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: uveitis, chorioretinitis

NE-20-J.t: Explain Ménière disease as endolymphatic hydrops causing episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: Ménière disease

NE-20-J.t: Explain acute otitis media (S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis) from eustachian tube dysfunction in children, otitis media with effusion, and complications including perforation, mastoiditis, cholesteatoma, and conductive hearing loss.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: otitis media, serous otitis, suppurative otitis, mastoiditis

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish otitis externa (Pseudomonas or S. aureus, pain with tragal pressure) from malignant otitis externa (Pseudomonas skull base osteomyelitis in older diabetics, cranial nerve palsies) and auricular perichondritis after cartilage piercing.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the ear: otitis externa, malignant otitis externa, chondritis

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish vestibular neuritis (acute continuous vertigo for days with normal hearing), labyrinthitis (vertigo with hearing loss), and benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (otoconia in the posterior canal, brief positional vertigo, positive Dix-Hallpike test).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Cranial nerve injury/disorders: vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis; Disorders of the ear: vertigo, otitis interna

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish central retinal artery occlusion (sudden painless monocular loss, pale retina, cherry-red spot), amaurosis fugax from carotid emboli, and central retinal vein occlusion (retinal hemorrhages and venous engorgement).

NE-20-J.t: Identify findings of hypertensive retinopathy (arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots), diabetic retinopathy (microaneurysms, hard exudates, neovascularization), and papilledema from raised intracranial pressure.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the retina: hypertensive retinopathy, retinal hemorrhage, papilledema

NE-20-J.t: Describe retinal detachment (flashes, floaters, curtain-like vision loss, myopia as a risk) and retinitis pigmentosa (inherited photoreceptor degeneration with night blindness, peripheral vision loss, and bone spicule pigment).
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the retina: retinal detachment, retinitis pigmentosa

NE-20-J.t: Explain myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, and presbyopia (age-related loss of lens elasticity), and relate childhood strabismus to amblyopia from cortical suppression of the deviating eye.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: refractive disorders, amblyopia, strabismus

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish conductive hearing loss (cerumen impaction, tympanic membrane perforation, barotrauma, eustachian tube dysfunction, otosclerosis with stapes fixation, cholesteatoma) from sensorineural loss (presbycusis, noise-induced hair cell damage), and relate both to tinnitus.

NE-20-J.t: Distinguish preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis from orbital cellulitis (pain with eye movement, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, usually from ethmoid sinusitis), and describe dacryocystitis and endophthalmitis.
NE-20-J.usmle: Nervous System: Disorders of the eye: periorbital cellulitis, dacryocystitis, endophthalmitis

NE-20-J.t: Describe pterygium as UV-related fibrovascular conjunctival growth onto the cornea, and lens dislocation in Marfan syndrome (usually upward) and homocystinuria (usually downward).
